title: OdrÃ­a Consolidates Military Rule
description: General Manuel OdrÃ­a solidifies authoritarian rule through the National Security Law, criminalizing APRA and Communist parties. His regime pursues export-led growth while political opponents face exile and censorship. Urban public works funded by the commodity boom cultivate a working-class support base.

title: Peru Anchovy Fisheries Boom Begins
description: Peru's Pacific anchovy fisheries enter a period of explosive growth, attracting large investment in processing plants along the coast from Paita to Ilo. The industry creates tens of thousands of jobs but exerts mounting pressure on the Humboldt Current ecosystem. Within a decade Peru becomes the world's largest fishmeal producer.

title: Women Gain Voting Rights in Peru
description: Peru grants women the right to vote in national elections for the first time, though the reform initially applies only to literate women, excluding large numbers of indigenous and rural women. The measure is widely seen as a tactical move by OdrÃ­a to expand his electorate. Formal political inclusion of women marks a significant shift in Peruvian civic life.

title: Nixon Visit Sparks Anti-U.S. Protests in Lima
description: U.S. Vice President Richard Nixon's Lima visit in May 1958 triggers violent protests by students opposing American support for Latin American military dictatorships. Nixon's motorcade is attacked by stone-throwing demonstrators, becoming an international incident. The protests reflect growing nationalist and anti-Cold War sentiment across Peru.

title: La ConvenciÃ³n Valley Peasant Mobilizations
description: Trotskyist organizer Hugo Blanco leads land occupations and strikes against the hacienda system in Cusco's La ConvenciÃ³n valley, one of Peru's most significant rural mobilizations. Blanco helps peasants form unions and resist landlord demands, inspiring similar movements elsewhere. The uprising becomes a reference point for debates about revolutionary strategy in Peru.

title: Military Coup Prevents APRA Electoral Victory
description: Following inconclusive elections in June 1962 with APRA poised to form a government, the military stages a coup on July 18, annulling results and citing alleged fraud. The junta, led by General Ricardo PÃ©rez Godoy, schedules new elections. The coup reveals deep military hostility toward APRA and the armed forces' self-appointed role as political guardians.

title: Fernando BelaÃºnde Terry Elected President
description: Fernando BelaÃºnde Terry wins the 1963 election with a reformist platform promising agrarian reform, infrastructure development, and integration of indigenous highlands into national life. His Andean regionalism and emphasis on Inca heritage represent a departure from APRA's coastal nationalism. The election ends the military interregnum and restores civilian rule.

title: MIR and ELN Guerrilla Insurgencies Suppressed
description: The Movement of the Revolutionary Left and Army of National Liberation simultaneously launch armed operations in highland and jungle regions, inspired by the Cuban model. Both insurgencies are crushed by late 1965 through military counterinsurgency operations, with their leaderships decimated. The failures provoke debate on armed struggle versus political organizing that shapes Sendero Luminoso's emergence.

title: Velasco Alvarado Military Coup and Revolution
description: On October 3, 1968, General Juan Velasco Alvarado overthrows President BelaÃºnde and establishes the Revolutionary Government of the Armed Forces, launching the Peruvian Revolution. Unlike previous coups, this intervention is motivated by nationalist-reformist ideology viewing structural change as necessary for national development. The junta immediately announces sweeping agrarian, industrial, and resource policy reforms.

title: IPC Expropriation: Talara Act Asserts Oil Sovereignty
description: Days after seizing power, the Velasco government expropriates the International Petroleum Company's La Brea y PariÃ±as refinery through the Act of Talara, fulfilling a decades-old nationalist demand. The move generates enormous popular enthusiasm and signals willingness to confront U.S. corporate interests. The U.S. government responds with diplomatic pressure and threatens the Hickenlooper Amendment.

title: Sweeping Agrarian Reform Dismantles Hacienda System
description: Decree Law 17716 expropriates all haciendas above a size threshold and transfers approximately 8.6 million hectares to peasant cooperatives and smallholders, ending a four-century social order. Military officers personally preside over symbolic handover ceremonies in highland communities. Though historically significant, cooperative productivity outcomes prove disappointing in subsequent years.

title: Ancash Earthquake Kills 70,000 People
description: A magnitude 7.9 earthquake strikes Ancash on May 31, 1970, triggering landslides that bury the city of Yungay and surrounding towns, killing an estimated 66,000 to 70,000 people in one of the deadliest disasters in Western Hemisphere history. International relief operations are mobilized as Peru's emergency capacity is overwhelmed. The disaster exposes the vulnerability of highland populations and the inadequacy of existing infrastructure.

title: Fisheries Nationalization Coincides with Anchoveta Collapse
description: The Velasco government nationalizes the fishmeal industry and creates state enterprise Pesca PerÃº just as the anchovy catch collapses due to overfishing and a severe El NiÃ±o event disrupting the Humboldt Current. The state inherits an industry at the peak of over-exploitation, devastating Peru's leading export earner. The simultaneous nationalization and ecological collapse becomes one of the costliest mistakes of the Velasco era.

title: Sendero Luminoso Consolidates in Ayacucho
description: Abimael GuzmÃ¡n, a philosophy professor at the University of Huamanga, builds the Communist Party of Peruâ€“Shining Path into a clandestine Maoist organization through systematic ideological indoctrination in highland communities. GuzmÃ¡n constructs a cult of personality as the fourth sword of Marxism, combining Maoist people's war doctrine with an apocalyptic revolutionary vision. The organization's penetration of universities and rural communities creates the base for its subsequent armed campaign.

title: Morales BermÃºdez Coup Ends Radical Military Revolution
description: On August 29, 1975, General Francisco Morales BermÃºdez overthrows the ailing Velasco in an internal military coup, ending the radical phase of the Peruvian Revolution and beginning his proclaimed Second Phase of moderation. Morales BermÃºdez reverses many of Velasco's most radical measures and reopens Peru to engagement with international financial institutions. The coup ends the most ambitious experiment in reformist military governance in Latin American history.

title: IMF Stabilization Program Imposes Austerity
description: The Morales BermÃºdez government negotiates a stabilization agreement with the IMF, committing Peru to fiscal adjustment, currency devaluation, and wage restraint in exchange for balance-of-payments support. The measures trigger a deep recession and sharp falls in real wages, generating significant social conflict and strikes. The episode introduces Peru to the austerity politics that will recur in subsequent economic crises.

title: General Strike Forces Democratic Transition Announcement
description: A general strike in July 1977, the largest in Peruvian history to that point, paralyzes the country as workers protest wage freezes and social spending cuts under the IMF program. The strike's success demonstrates organized labor's strength despite a decade of military rule. Morales BermÃºdez responds by announcing a transition to democracy and scheduling constituent assembly elections.

title: Constituent Assembly Grants Universal Suffrage
description: Peru's constituent assembly elected in June 1978 drafts a new constitution granting voting rights to all citizens regardless of literacy, incorporating millions of indigenous and rural Peruvians into the formal democratic system for the first time. APRA wins the largest share of seats, with Haya de la Torre elected assembly president. The constitution fundamentally reshapes Peru's electoral politics by enfranchising previously excluded populations.

title: Sendero Luminoso Launches Armed Campaign
description: On May 17, 1980, the night before Peru's return to democratic elections, Sendero Luminoso burns ballot boxes in the Ayacucho village of Chuschi, launching its People's War insurgency. The timing is deliberately symbolic, rejecting electoral democracy as a sham. The campaign grows into one of the bloodiest internal conflicts in Latin American history, ultimately killing approximately 69,000 Peruvians.

title: BelaÃºnde Returns in Democratic Elections
description: Fernando BelaÃºnde Terry wins the 1980 presidential election, becoming the first democratically elected president to succeed a military government in Peruvian history. His second government pursues economic liberalization and engagement with international financial institutions, reversing Velasco-era statism. The transition represents a historic restoration of civilian democratic governance.

title: Military Enters Counterinsurgency Against Sendero
description: As Sendero Luminoso's attacks escalate and police prove incapable of containment, the BelaÃºnde government declares a state of emergency in Ayacucho and deploys the military with broad powers. The army's approach involves collective punishment of communities suspected of supporting Sendero, generating hundreds of extrajudicial killings. Military tactics sometimes drive communities toward Sendero rather than away from it.

title: MRTA Founded as Second Guerrilla Organization
description: The TÃºpac Amaru Revolutionary Movement is formally founded by former APRA youth and Marxists who reject both orthodox communism and Sendero's Maoism, naming themselves after an eighteenth-century indigenous rebel leader. The MRTA espouses nationalist leftism and explicitly seeks to avoid targeting civilians, distinguishing itself from Sendero. Despite this stance, the organization conducts bank robberies, kidnappings, and political assassinations throughout the decade.

title: Ayacucho Massacres Document Systematic Atrocities
description: Peruvian security forces conduct a series of massacres of highland communities suspected of supporting Sendero Luminoso, including killings in Socos and Pucayacu, later documented by the Truth and Reconciliation Commission as crimes against humanity. Forced disappearances become systematic, with detained individuals vanishing without official acknowledgment. Human rights organizations begin documenting abuses that receive little official response.

title: Alan GarcÃ­a Elected: APRA's First Presidency
description: Alan GarcÃ­a wins the 1985 election with 53 percent of the first-round vote, giving APRA its first ever access to the presidency after six decades as Peru's dominant opposition party. GarcÃ­a's personal charisma and widespread desire for change after BelaÃºnde's disappointing second term combine to produce a landslide. His government will become one of the most economically catastrophic in Peru's modern history.

title: GarcÃ­a Limits Debt Service to 10% of Export Revenue
description: In a dramatic act of economic nationalism, President GarcÃ­a announces Peru will limit debt service payments to 10 percent of export revenue, unilaterally renegotiating its relationship with international creditors. The declaration leads to Peru's exclusion from international capital markets, with the IMF declaring the country ineligible for assistance. The short-term debt relief is more than offset by the subsequent collapse of investment and foreign exchange access.

title: El FrontÃ³n Prison Massacre
description: Peruvian security forces kill approximately 250 to 300 Sendero Luminoso prisoners at three Lima prisons on June 18â€“19, 1986, most after they had already surrendered in the coordinated uprising they initiated. The massacre is subsequently documented as a series of extrajudicial executions. The episode occurs during the APRA International Socialist meeting in Lima, drawing intense international attention and embarrassing the GarcÃ­a government.

title: Hyperinflation Reaches Crisis Levels Under GarcÃ­a
description: Peru's economy enters hyperinflationary collapse in 1988, with annual inflation reaching 1,722 percent and rising further to nearly 3,000 percent in 1989, one of the most severe episodes in Latin American history. The collapse of GarcÃ­a's heterodox program wipes out savings and destroys the domestic financial system. Real wages collapse by more than 60 percent and poverty soars, leaving the Peruvian state unable to deliver basic services across much of the country.

title: Fujimori Defeats Vargas Llosa in Presidential Runoff
description: Alberto Fujimori defeats novelist Mario Vargas Llosa in the June 1990 presidential runoff with approximately 62 percent of the vote, winning one of the most dramatic electoral upsets in Latin American history. Fujimori benefited from APRA's tactical support and mobilization of indigenous, evangelical, and lower-class urban voters who identified with his outsider status. The result marks a decisive rejection of Peru's traditional political class by a newly empowered electorate.

title: Fujishock: Economic Shock Therapy Ends Hyperinflation
description: Days after taking office on July 28, 1990, Fujimori implements a severe economic shock programâ€”contradicting his campaign pledgeâ€”through drastic fiscal adjustment, price liberalization, and monetary stabilization. The fujishock produces an immediate recession but successfully breaks the hyperinflationary dynamic, with monthly inflation falling from triple-digit rates to single digits within months. The stabilization creates the foundation for Peru's economic recovery through the 1990s.

title: Cholera Epidemic Exposes Public Health Collapse
description: A severe cholera epidemic erupts in January 1991, the first in the Western Hemisphere in a century, spreading rapidly from coastal fishing communities through Lima's slums and into highland and Amazonian regions, infecting hundreds of thousands and killing thousands. The epidemic exposes catastrophic deficiencies in water, sanitation, and public health infrastructure resulting from a decade of economic crisis and neglected investment. International emergency assistance is mobilized, but structural vulnerabilities persist.

title: Autogolpe: Fujimori Dissolves Congress and Courts
description: On April 5, 1992, President Fujimori dissolves Congress, suspends the Constitution, and closes the judiciary in a self-coup backed by the military, citing congressional obstruction of counter-terrorism programs. The move is condemned internationally by the OAS but receives significant domestic popular support from Peruvians frustrated with governmental dysfunction and escalating Sendero attacks. The autogolpe fundamentally transforms Fujimori's government toward competitive authoritarianism.

title: Capture of Abimael GuzmÃ¡n Breaks Sendero Luminoso
description: On September 12, 1992, police intelligence unit GEIN arrests Abimael GuzmÃ¡n and Sendero Luminoso's top leadership in a Lima safe house, one of the most significant counterterrorism successes in Latin American history. GuzmÃ¡n's capture is the result of patient intelligence work focusing on urban support networks. The loss of its theoretician and charismatic leader deals a catastrophic blow to the organization and triggers its internal collapse.

title: Fujimori's New Constitution Entrenches Presidential Power
description: A constituent congress drafts and voters approve a new constitution in October 1993 that significantly strengthens presidential power, introduces the possibility of reelection, reduces Congress to one chamber, and establishes a framework for economic liberalization. The constitution provides legal legitimacy for Fujimori's authoritarian project while giving him structural electoral advantages. Critics argue the drafting process was controlled by Fujimori loyalists and the referendum manipulated.

title: Economic Boom Driven by Mining Privatization
description: Peru experiences rapid GDP growth exceeding 12 percent in 1994â€“1995 as foreign investment flows into telecommunications, electricity, and mining following mass privatization of state enterprises. Canadian, U.S., and Australian mining firms invest heavily, attracted by Peru's liberalized mining law and rich geological endowment. Urban middle-class living standards improve visibly, though benefits reach the rural poor much more slowly.

title: Cenepa War with Ecuador Over Border Dispute
description: Peru and Ecuador fight a brief but intense border war in the Cenepa valley in Januaryâ€“February 1995, the most significant armed conflict between the two countries since 1941. The better-equipped Peruvian military achieves superiority, and the war ends with a cease-fire brokered by the United States, Brazil, Argentina, and Chile. The conflict temporarily boosts Fujimori's popularity and is definitively resolved by the 1998 BrasÃ­lia peace agreement.

title: Amnesty Law Shields Military from Human Rights Prosecution
description: Congress passes an amnesty law in June 1995 granting immunity from prosecution for all military and police human rights violations committed between 1980 and 1995, covering cases including Barrios Altos and La Cantuta. The law triggers widespread domestic and international condemnation and is subsequently found by the Inter-American Court of Human Rights to be incompatible with Peru's international obligations. The law represents the Fujimori government's systematic effort to protect the security apparatus from accountability.

title: MRTA Seizes Japanese Embassy Hostages
description: On December 17, 1996, MRTA militants seize the Japanese ambassador's residence during a reception, taking 72 hostages including government ministers, ambassadors, and business leaders. The dramatic hostage-taking draws global media attention and places the Fujimori government under intense pressure. Negotiations drag on for months as the MRTA demands the release of imprisoned comrades and Fujimori refuses all concessions.

title: Japanese Embassy Rescue Operation Ends Hostage Crisis
description: On April 22, 1997, Peruvian special forces tunnel under the ambassador's residence and launch a sudden assault, killing all 14 MRTA members and rescuing all but one of the 72 hostages. The operationâ€”code-named ChavÃ­n de HuÃ¡ntarâ€”produces a significant surge in Fujimori's popularity. Subsequent investigations reveal several MRTA members were executed after surrendering, but these findings do not reduce the immediate political impact.

title: El NiÃ±o Causes Catastrophic Flooding and Economic Losses
description: One of the strongest El NiÃ±o events of the twentieth century devastates Peru's northern coastal agricultural zones, fishing industry, and infrastructure in 1997â€“1998, causing catastrophic flooding and collapse of the anchovy stock. Economic losses reach an estimated $3.5 billion, representing several percentage points of GDP. The disaster exposes the continued structural vulnerability of Peru's economy to climate variability.

title: Vladivideo Scandal Brings Down Fujimori Regime
description: In September 2000, the release of a video showing intelligence chief Vladimiro Montesinos paying $15,000 to a congressman triggers a political earthquake, exposing the systematic corruption sustaining Fujimori's rule. Montesinos flees Peru, and Fujimori travels to the APEC summit and then Japan, submitting his resignation via fax and claiming Japanese citizenship to avoid extradition. The regime's spectacular collapse ends a decade of authoritarian rule.

title: Alejandro Toledo Elected Peru's First Indigenous President
description: Alejandro Toledo wins the 2001 presidential election against former president Alan GarcÃ­a, becoming Peru's first president of indigenous Andean descent and symbolically fulfilling the democratic promise of the 1978 universal suffrage reform. Toledo campaigns on his rags-to-riches biography and Quechua origins alongside Stanford-trained economist credentials. His election generates genuine popular enthusiasm though the government proves administratively weak.

title: Truth and Reconciliation Commission: 69,000 Conflict Dead
description: The Truth and Reconciliation Commission releases its landmark nine-volume final report in August 2003, concluding that approximately 69,280 people were killed or forcibly disappeared during the 1980â€“2000 internal armed conflict. The report attributes the largest share of killings to Shining Path but also documents systematic army atrocities. Its finding that indigenous, Quechua-speaking rural populations bore the greatest burden provokes deep national reflection on Peru's racial and regional inequalities.

title: Mining Boom Sparks Growing Community Conflicts
description: Rising commodity prices accelerate Peru's mining sector expansion, attracting large foreign investments in Cajamarca, Ancash, and Puno. However, conflicts between mining companies and local communities over water resources, environmental contamination, and royalty distribution become increasingly common. The government lacks adequate mechanisms for community consultation or conflict resolution, establishing a pattern of recurring extractive-sector crises.

title: Alan GarcÃ­a Returns to Presidency with Centrist Platform
description: Alan GarcÃ­a defeats Ollanta Humala in the 2006 presidential runoff, staging a remarkable comeback from his disastrous first presidency by campaigning as a pro-market social democrat who explicitly disavows his earlier economic nationalism. Peruvian voters ultimately choose the known quantity of GarcÃ­a over the uncertain nationalism of Humala. His second term proves far more economically orthodox, governing Peru during a period of rapid commodity-driven growth.

title: Peru Economy Grows 9.8% Amid Commodity Boom
description: Peru's economy expands at approximately 9.8 percent in 2008, driven by surging copper, gold, silver, and zinc exports alongside strong domestic demand and investment. The national poverty rate falls from about 55 percent in 2001 to below 40 percent by 2008. However, growth remains heavily concentrated geographically, with highland and Amazonian regions benefiting far less than Lima and coastal urban areas.

title: Bagua Massacre: Indigenous Amazonian Protest Turns Deadly
description: On June 5, 2009, a confrontation near Bagua between indigenous protesters blocking a highway and police attempting to clear it results in 23 police and at least 10 indigenous civilian deaths. The conflict erupts from months of protests against GarcÃ­a's Amazon development decrees promoted over indigenous land rights. National outrage forces the government to repeal the contested decrees, but tensions between indigenous rights and extractive development persist.

title: Fujimori Convicted of Human Rights Violations
description: A special criminal tribunal convicts former president Alberto Fujimori of kidnapping and murder in connection with the Barrios Altos and La Cantuta massacres, sentencing him to 25 years in prison. The verdict is celebrated as a landmark achievement for accountability in Latin America, demonstrating that former heads of state can be held responsible for atrocities committed during their administrations. Peru's prosecution of Fujimori without reliance on an international tribunal sets an important regional precedent.

title: Ollanta Humala Wins Presidential Election
description: Ollanta Humala defeats Keiko Fujimori in the 2011 presidential runoff with 51.5 percent of the vote, running a more moderate campaign than in 2006 and signing a commitment to the existing economic model. His election provokes significant business anxiety despite his moderation, given his political career built on opposition to the neoliberal consensus. The result represents the victory of a candidate drawing support from historically marginalized highland, Amazonian, and impoverished urban populations.

title: Conga Mining Project Conflict in Cajamarca
description: Protests erupt in Cajamarca against the proposed Conga gold and copper project, with communities arguing it would destroy four high-altitude lagoons supplying regional water. The conflict becomes the defining social confrontation of Humala's presidency, testing his commitment to both extractive development revenues and community rights. The government declares states of emergency and ultimately suspends the project indefinitely, satisfying neither side.

title: Odebrecht Corruption Begins to Surface in Peru
description: Evidence surfaces in Brazil of construction giant Odebrecht's massive bribery scheme across Latin America, with Peru identified as a country where the company paid officials approximately $29 million to secure infrastructure contracts including the InteroceÃ¡nica highway and Lima metro. The full magnitude is revealed in 2016 when Odebrecht executives begin cooperating with Brazilian prosecutors. The scandal will implicate every living former president and fundamentally delegitimize Peru's political establishment.

title: Kuczynski Wins Narrow Election Amid Fujimori Hostility
description: Pedro Pablo Kuczynski narrowly defeats Keiko Fujimori in the 2016 presidential runoff with just 50.1 percent of the vote, initiating acute political instability as Fujimori's Fuerza Popular wins a congressional majority. The confrontational executiveâ€“legislative dynamic defined by Fujimori's strategic use of censure and impeachment threats characterizes Peruvian politics for the next five years. The election reflects deep polarization between Fujimorismo and its opponents.

title: El NiÃ±o Costero Causes Catastrophic Coastal Flooding
description: An unusual coastal El NiÃ±o event in early 2017 causes catastrophic flooding and landslides across Peru's northern and central coastal regions, killing over 100 people and destroying thousands of homes. The disaster disrupts agricultural production, isolates highland communities, and causes economic losses estimated at several billion dollars. Recovery is politically contentious, with accusations of government mismanagement and delayed reconstruction funding.

title: Kuczynski Pardons Fujimori Then Resigns Amid Corruption
description: Kuczynski grants a widely condemned humanitarian pardon to jailed former dictator Alberto Fujimori in December 2017, with critics alleging it was a quid pro quo for legislative votes saving his government. Massive protests condemn the pardon, a second impeachment motion advances, and Kuczynski resigns on March 21, 2018, becoming the first Peruvian president to resign over corruption allegations. First Vice President MartÃ­n Vizcarra assumes the presidency.

title: Vizcarra Dissolves Congress in Constitutional Standoff
description: After Congress refuses to confirm a Constitutional Tribunal member, President Vizcarra dissolves it on September 30, 2019, invoking a provision allowing dissolution when the legislature has twice denied cabinet confidence. Congressional leaders contest the action, briefly declaring Vizcarra suspended and attempting to swear in the first vice president. The Constitutional Tribunal upholds the dissolution, and new elections produce a fragmented legislature in January 2020.

title: Former Presidents Prosecuted in Odebrecht Cases
description: Criminal proceedings against Peru's former presidents intensify: Toledo becomes a fugitive seeking asylum in the United States; Alan GarcÃ­a shoots himself when police arrive to detain him in April 2019 and dies shortly afterward; Humala and his wife are briefly jailed before release pending trial. The simultaneous legal troubles of three former heads of state in a single corruption scandal has no precedent in Peruvian or regional history.

title: Peru Cycles Through Three Presidents in One Week
description: Peru undergoes an extraordinary political crisis in November 2020, cycling through three presidents in less than two weeks: Congress impeaches Vizcarra, installs Manuel Merino who resigns after massive protests kill two demonstrators, then appoints Francisco Sagasti as compromise president. The crisis occurs during the COVID-19 pandemic and draws international astonishment at the depth of Peru's political dysfunction. Public disillusionment with all institutional actors deepens markedly.

title: COVID-19 Pandemic: Peru Among World's Hardest Hit
description: Peru suffers one of the world's highest COVID-19 mortality rates, with excess deaths suggesting hundreds of thousands of deaths attributable to the pandemic. The health system collapses in multiple waves, with hospitals overwhelmed, oxygen critically scarce, and intensive care capacity far below demand. The catastrophic toll reflects decades of underinvestment in public health, extreme urban overcrowding, a large informal economy, and political dysfunction undermining coordinated response.

title: Pedro Castillo Wins Presidency from Rural Obscurity
description: Pedro Castillo, a rural schoolteacher and union leader from Cajamarca with no prior political office, wins the 2021 presidential election against Keiko Fujimori by fewer than 45,000 votes out of more than 17 million cast. His radical platform of constitutional change and resource nationalization frightens business and middle-class voters, while his Andean rural background generates enthusiastic support among historically marginalized populations. Months of fraud accusations follow before electoral authorities confirm the result.

title: Castillo Faces Multiple Impeachment Attempts
description: Congress initiates impeachment proceedings against Castillo multiple times in 2022, citing alleged corruption in public works contracts and broader accusations of moral incapacity. Castillo survives the first two votes as a divided Congress cannot muster the required two-thirds majority, while criminal investigations by the attorney general continue advancing. The repeated impeachment attempts without definitive result contribute to governmental paralysis and economic uncertainty.

title: Castillo's Self-Coup Attempt Leads to Impeachment and Arrest
description: On December 7, 2022, facing a third impeachment vote, Castillo announces dissolution of Congress and installation of an emergency governmentâ€”a self-coup attempt reminiscent of Fujimori's 1992 autogolpe. The attempt immediately collapses as the military and police refuse support, cabinet ministers resign, and Congress votes 101 to 47 to impeach him within hours. Castillo is arrested and First Vice President Dina Boluarte assumes the presidency.

title: Boluarte Government Kills Dozens of Protesters
description: The Boluarte government faces massive protests in highland and southern regions demanding Castillo's release and new elections, with security forces responding with live ammunition in multiple incidents at Ayacucho, Juliaca, and Puno. The death toll exceeds 60 protesters, prompting human rights organizations and international bodies including the OAS and UN to call for independent investigations. The killings fuel a deep legitimacy crisis that leaves Peru effectively ungoverned in much of the south.

title: Political Stalemate and Governance Paralysis Persist
description: President Dina Boluarte continues in office through 2024 despite approval ratings below 10 percent and ongoing criminal investigations into protest killings, while Congress is equally distrusted but lacks constitutional means to remove her without new elections. The stalemate produces governmental paralysis and underscores the failure of Peru's constitutional design to provide stable governance. Proposals for constitutional reform circulate without finding political consensus.

title: Organized Crime and Gang Violence Escalates
description: Peru experiences a significant escalation in organized crime and gang violence, with extortion networks targeting businesses, construction sites, and transport operators across Lima and coastal cities, with links to Venezuelan criminal organizations increasingly documented. Homicide rates rise in multiple cities, and the political class's failure to address public security becomes a major electoral issue ahead of the 2026 cycle. The deterioration is particularly acute in Callao and Lima districts with large informal-sector populations.
